content: 1. The Against Women Research Group conducted a randomized trial to evaluate the effectiveness of screening for intimate partner violence (IPV) in healthcare settings. This study highlights the importance of early detection and intervention in clinical environments. 2. Rhodes KV et al. explored the impact of lowering the threshold for discussions about domestic violence through a randomized controlled trial using computer-based screening. Their findings were published in the Archives of Internal Medicine in 2006. 3. Dua T et al. summarized evidence-based guidelines for managing mental, neurological, and substance use disorders in lowand middle-income countries, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). This work emphasizes the global need for accessible mental health care. 4. Kiely M et al. developed and tested an integrated intervention aimed at reducing IPV during pregnancy. Their study, published in Obstetrics and Gynecology in 2010, demonstrated the potential benefits of targeted support for pregnant women. 5. Ramsay J et al. conducted a systematic review of interventions designed to reduce violence and improve the physical and psychosocial well-being of women experiencing partner abuse. This review was commissioned by the UK Department of Health in 2006. 6. Sadowski L and Casteel C reviewed the prevalence and consequences of IPV against women, providing clinical evidence to guide healthcare providers in addressing this issue. 7. Bisson J et al. performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of psychological treatments for chronic post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), highlighting the effectiveness of evidence-based therapies. Their findings were published in the British Journal of Psychiatry in 2007. 8. Gilbert L et al. tested a combined relapse prevention and relationship safety intervention for women undergoing methadone treatment. Their study, published in Violence and Victims in 2006, examined the short-term effects on IPV and substance use. 9. Howard LM et al. reviewed the relationship between domestic violence and mental health, emphasizing the need for integrated care approaches. Their work appeared in the International Review of Psychiatry in 2010. 10. Kubany ES et al. introduced Cognitive Trauma Therapy for Battered Women with PTSD (CTT-BW) and reported preliminary findings in the Journal of Trauma and Stress in 2003. A follow-up study in 2004 further validated the therapy's effectiveness. 11. Lieberman AF et al. investigated child-parent psychotherapy for preschoolers exposed to marital violence. Their randomized controlled trial, published in the Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry in 2005, demonstrated significant benefits for both children and parents. 12. Zlotnick C et al. piloted an interpersonally-based intervention for low-income pregnant women experiencing IPV. Their findings, published in the Archives of Women’s Mental Health in 2011, highlighted the potential for improving maternal mental health and safety. 13. Bair-Merritt MH et al. evaluated the Hawaii Healthy Start Home Visitation Program, which aimed to reduce maternal IPV after childbirth. Their randomized controlled trial was published in the Archives of Pediatric and Adolescent Medicine in 2010. 14. Constantino R et al. assessed the effects of a social support intervention on health outcomes for residents of a domestic violence shelter. Their pilot study, published in Issues in Mental Health Nursing in 2005, demonstrated positive impacts on mental health and well-being. 15. Cripé SW et al. implemented a pilot intervention program addressing IPV during pregnancy in Lima, Peru. Their study, published in the Journal of Interpersonal Violence in 2010, provided insights into culturally tailored approaches. 16. Gillum TL et al. examined whether a health clinic-based intervention could enhance safety for abused women. Their pilot study, published in the Journal of Women’s Health in 2009, showed promising results. 17. Humphreys J et al. used a video doctor intervention combined with provider cueing to increase discussions about IPV during prenatal care. Their randomized controlled trial, published in Women’s Health Issues in 2011, demonstrated improved communication and outcomes. 18. McFarlane J et al. evaluated interventions to decrease IPV among pregnant women. Their findings, published in Public Health Nursing in 2000, emphasized the importance of secondary prevention strategies. 19. Franzblau SH et al. explored the effects of yogic breathing techniques and testimony on depression among battered women. Their preliminary investigation, published in the Journal of Interpersonal Violence in 2008, suggested potential therapeutic benefits. 20. Koopman CF et al. studied the impact of expressive writing on pain, depression, and PTSD symptoms in IPV survivors. Their findings, published in the Journal of Health Psychology in 2005, highlighted the value of creative therapeutic approaches. 21. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed clinical and policy guidelines for responding to IPV and sexual violence against women. These guidelines emphasize evidence-based practices for healthcare providers. 22. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists issued a practice bulletin on emergency contraception, providing guidance on its use in cases of sexual assault. 23. Abrahams N et al. investigated the role of telephonic psychosocial support in improving adherence to post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after rape. Their study, published in AIDS Care in 2010, highlighted the importance of support systems. 24. Resick PA et al. compared cognitive-processing therapy with prolonged exposure therapy for treating chronic PTSD in female rape victims. Their findings, published in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology in 2002, demonstrated the efficacy of both approaches. 25. Rothbaum BO conducted a controlled study on eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) for PTSD in sexual assault victims. The study, published in the Bulletin of the Menninger Clinic in 1997, provided evidence for EMDR's effectiveness.
